projects.title: Animatronic Eye Mech
projects.card: Two SG90 servos: one sweeps the eye 100°, one blinks both lids through a 12-tooth gear pair designed into the eyelids.

summary.Problem: Design a fully 3D-printed, compact animatronic eye driven by an Arduino and servo motors.
summary.My role: Personal project: research, SolidWorks design, printing, assembly and Arduino code
summary.Size: 80 × 84 × 59 mm with the servo stand (about 3 in at the base); Ø64 mm eyeball
summary.Tools: SolidWorks, Bambu Lab A1 (PLA), Arduino C++, two SG90 micro servos
summary.Result: Working eye (iteration 3, joints repaired) that blinks and looks left and right

sections.heading: Approach
items: Researched existing eye mechs and brainstormed ideas to make them more compact. Prioritized mounting the servos within the eye, making the design self-contained.

items.text: Eye movement: the eyeball needed to look left and right.
items: A central arm connects directly to an SG90 micro servo and rotates the eye left and right.

items.text: Geared eyelids: the eyelids needed to blink without multiple servos or large linkages.
items: Custom gears are designed directly into the upper and lower eyelids. The gears mesh, so the lids always open and close together and only one eyelid needs to be driven by a servo.

items.text: Self-contained eyelid drive: the servo needed to mount within the eye cavity.
items: The eyelid servo mounts on a frame inside the eye, keeping the whole mechanism compact. A curved two-bar linkage reaches up and over the eyeball to the top of the upper eyelid, shaped to stay clear of the eyeball as it rotates left and right.

sections.heading: Specs (from the final CAD, v3)
items: Overall: 80 × 84 × 59 mm including the servo test stand; 10 parts in the final assembly.
Eyeball: Ø64 mm sphere with a 1.0 mm wall. Eyelids: 72 mm wide, 1.0 mm shells.

items.text: Eyelid gears: a 1:1 spur pair cut into the eyelid hubs, so one servo drives both lids.
items: 12 teeth, module 0.8, 20° pressure angle
Ø9.6 mm pitch, Ø11.2 mm tip, 9.6 mm center distance
Eyelid linkage: 30.0 mm crank on the lid servo and a curved 26.79 mm coupler (R35 mm arc) that reaches over the eyeball to the upper lid.
Clearances: lid bores Ø3.0 mm on Ø2.5 mm pivots (0.5 mm diametral clearance); the upper lid has a 1.5 mm slot for the Ø2.0 mm hinge pin.
Servos: two SG90 micro servos, one for the eyeball and one for the eyelids, both packed into the hollow back of the eyeball.
Printing: PLA on a Bambu Lab A1, 0.2 mm layers.

items.text: First iteration: the print-in-place gears were too small and the teeth fused together. The test stand was not stable enough to support the rotational inertia from the servos.
items: CAD v1: 10-tooth gears (Ø7.0 mm tip) with Ø2.5 mm bores on Ø2.5 mm pivots, so zero clearance; 68 mm lids.

items.text: Second iteration: incorrect tolerancing prevented the two-bar linkage from securely connecting to the eyelid. The servos were not properly secured to the test stand.
items: CAD v2: 12 teeth at module 0.5 (Ø6.0 mm pitch); bores opened to Ø3.0 mm on the same Ø2.5 mm pivots (0.5 mm clearance).

items.text: Third iteration: resized the gear teeth, added cross braces to the test stand, added a slot to the eyelid, and added screw holes to secure the servos. The mechanism worked, but the linkage joints were too small and broke during assembly. I repaired them with duct tape; this repaired third iteration is the eye in the video.
items: CAD v3: same 12 teeth scaled up to module 0.8 (Ø9.6 mm pitch, pivots 6.0 → 9.6 mm apart); lids widened 68 → 72 mm.

sections.heading: Code
items: Arduino C++, adapted from a SparkFun Inventor's Kit servo example (Circuit 3A).
Three push buttons: look left, look right and blink.
Look: the eyeball servo moves between 40° and 140° (a 100° sweep). While a button is held, each 10 ms step covers 5% of the remaining distance, so the eye starts fast and eases into the end position.

Blink: the lid servo goes from 20° to 70°. Each 10 ms step multiplies the angle by 1.1 to close and divides by 1.1 to open, which gives an eased motion. Computed from the code: about 140 ms to close, a 100 ms hold and about 140 ms to open, so one blink takes about 0.4 s.

sections.heading: Result
items: A working animatronic eye, about 3 in at the base, that blinks and looks left and right with two SG90 micro servos mounted in the back of the eye. I tested the full mechanism on the printed servo test stand.
The eye has since been taken apart. The video, the SolidWorks files and the Arduino sketch are the record of the build.

sections.heading: What I'd improve next
items: Increase the outer diameter of the linkage joints so they do not break when the pins are inserted.
Fix an overshoot bug in the blink: the close loop stops only after the angle passes 70°, so the last ×1.1 step reaches about 76°. The loop should clamp the angle to the 70° limit.
Add running clearance where the CAD is line-to-line: the Ø2.0 mm hinge pin sits in a Ø2.0 mm hole, and the eyelid shells (R32 mm inside) sit on the eyeball (R32 mm outside).

sections.heading: What I learned
items: Advanced assemblies in SolidWorks
Designing linkages and slots for dynamic motion and simpler assembly
Creating organic servo motion with custom Arduino code

projects.title: Vacuum Form Tray Study
projects.card: Found why PET vacuum-formed game trays cracked; the new standard passed QA drop tests, est. ~$120k/year on one title.

summary.Problem: Vacuum-formed game packaging trays were cracking. Find the root cause and a large-scale, cost-effective fix.
summary.My role: Project Engineer Co-op, Hasbro (Games, Play-Doh, NERF): assigned the investigation, root cause and fix
summary.Method: Hands-on inspection of failed trays, material review from supplier quotes, analysis of Hasbro QA drop-test results
summary.Result: New-standard trays passed QA drop tests; estimated ~$120k/year in savings on one title made in the millions

sections.heading: Background
items: Game packaging trays are vacuum-formed PET inserts that sit in the box and hold all of a board game's components.
Trays from several games were failing, and the goal was a large-scale, cost-effective fix.

sections.heading: Failure mode and root cause
items: Failure mode: the trays cracked.

items.text: Root cause: two things weakened the trays.
items: The corners were too stiff to flex and absorb impact.
Small decorative patterns on the top of the tray weakened the material around the edges.

sections.heading: How I investigated
items: Inspected every failed tray by hand, touching and flexing it.
Read the supplier quotes for each product to find out which materials were used.
Compared the failed trays with each other to find what they had in common.
Analyzed the results of Hasbro QA's internal drop tests. QA ran the tests; I analyzed the results.
Reported the findings to management in a detailed PowerPoint presentation.

sections.heading: The fix
items: Larger corner radii, so the corners flex more and cushion the components in the box.
Thinner material: many trays still failed at the maximum #32 gauge, so thicker material was not the answer.
Corrugated corner protectors in the master cartons, which cost less than thickening the tray material.

sections.heading: Result
items: Trays built to the new standard passed Hasbro QA's drop tests.
Estimated ~$120k/year in savings on one title, a game made in the millions.
Wrote tray design standards for future Hasbro Games trays.

sections.heading: What I learned
items: Working through a root cause analysis, from failed parts to a fix
Writing reports that compare many different metrics

projects.title: BenchPress: Hand-Crank Folding Picnic Table
projects.card: My part of a 5-person design: frame stress and Goodman fatigue that set the frame steel, the frame-to-brace bolt, and the team's part CAD.

summary.Problem: Design a folding picnic table whose legs fold out with a hand crank and gearbox (no motor).
summary.My role: Frame and brace stress and fatigue, frame-to-brace bolt, the team's part CAD and 3D printing
summary.Design assumptions: 1000 lb total load; target safety factor 2

projects.intro: This was a class design project. No physical prototype was built or tested. The numbers below come from hand calculations in the team's final report.

sections.heading: The design
items: A 72 in × 30 in tabletop with two 72 in benches. The legs swing out from the folded position.
A 6 in hand crank drives a 2-stage spur gearbox to raise the legs. The input is set at 5 lbf, the ADA minimum force to open a door.
Design assumptions: at most 1000 lb on the table and benches, and a safety factor of 2.

sections.heading: My part: frame and brace stress (report §2.1)
items: Drew the free-body diagrams of the bench frame and its 45° brace. Each side of the frame carries one 200 lb point load; I analyzed one side by symmetry.

items.text: Brace: a 1 in × 0.125 in bar at 45°, treated as a two-force member.
items: Brace force F_BD = 100 / sin 45° = 141.42 lb; axial stress 1131.4 psi.

items.text: Frame: a hollow steel tube, 2 in OD and 1.875 in ID.
items: Combined axial (526.3 psi) and bending stress from the brace (5036.5 psi) gives a required Sy of 11,125.6 psi at SF 2.
The report's brace buckling check is not shown here: it used steel's modulus for what became an aluminum brace. See "What I'd check next".

sections.heading: My part: fatigue and material selection (report §2.2)
items: Load case: people sitting down and standing up, so the load cycles 0 → 200 lb per person. Designed for infinite life.
Applied Marin factors to the endurance limit and used the modified Goodman criterion with n = 2.
Required ultimate strength: 5551 psi for the brace and 32,047 psi for the frame. Fatigue, not static stress, drove the frame material.
Selected AISI 1006 hot-rolled steel for the frame (Sut 43 ksi, Sy 24 ksi) and 2017-O aluminum for the brace (Sut 26 ksi, Sy 10 ksi); the brace material was chosen on fatigue alone.

sections.heading: My part: frame-to-brace bolt (report §3.3)
items: A 1/4 in-28 UNF bolt in pure shear carries the 141.42 lb brace force. I sized its length (2.25 in) and thread length from the grip.
Shear stress 4338 psi. A Grade 5 bolt gives a safety factor of 12.24, far more than needed.
Downgraded to Grade 1 (n = 4.8), which still clears the SF 2 target and costs less.

sections.heading: My part: CAD and 3D printing
items: Modeled the team's SolidWorks parts and assemblies: bench arm, table arm, tabletop, bench seat and the scaled full assembly (146.9 × 58.9 × 88 mm, 7 parts).
Did all the 3D printing: a test arm, test cylinders and arm caps in several sizes. The v2 table arm opened the pivot bore from Ø7 to Ø8 mm.

sections.heading: Team work (not my sections)
items: Teammates designed the hand-crank 2-stage gearbox (12T → 60T spur stages), sized the tabletop and bench seats, and checked the welds and the tabletop bolts.

sections.heading: What I'd check next
items: Re-check the brace for buckling. The team's check used Johnson's formula with steel's modulus (30 × 10⁶ psi), but the brace chosen later is 2017-O aluminum (about 10.5 × 10⁶ psi), and a brace this slender is governed by Euler's formula. With aluminum it likely falls below a safety factor of 1, so the fix would be a steel brace or a thicker bar.
Build and load-test a full-size frame and brace. Nothing in this project was physically tested.

projects.title: Robotic Treasure Chest
projects.card: Servo-driven custom bevel gears open the lid in sync with a piezo melody.

summary.Problem: Design a fully 3D-printed storage chest with Arduino electronics to make an interactive desk toy.
summary.My role: Personal project: mechanism design, CAD, printing, electronics and Arduino code
summary.Tools: SolidWorks, 3D printing, Arduino C++, servo motor, piezo buzzer
summary.Result: Working desk toy whose custom gear assembly opens the chest in sync with the classic Legend of Zelda tune

items.text: Brainstormed and prototyped several opening mechanisms based on the Arduino components available.
items: First iteration: a servo with a custom spool tensioned a string from inside the chest. The lid could not open at different speeds; it only opened rapidly once enough tension built up.

Second iteration: custom bevel gears driven by the servo, attached to the back of the chest near the hinge. This allowed more dynamic movement, but the assembly was too fragile and broke during adjustments.
Third iteration: improved tolerances and hinge design for easier installation and lower stress on the gears and hinges.

sections.heading: Specs (from the final CAD)
items: Overall: 70 × 75 × 67 mm with the lid closed; 5 parts (base, lid, servo and two gears).
Drive: the servo turns a pair of 12-tooth straight bevel gears with 45° cones (a 1:1 miter pair at 90°, Ø16.1 mm). The second gear sits on the lid's hinge axis, so the servo rotates the lid directly.
Hinge: Ø3.8 mm pins on the lid sit in Ø4.0 mm open hooks on the base (0.2 mm diametral clearance), replacing the first version's separate bolt.
Walls: 2.0 mm lid shell and 2.0 mm base walls.

sections.heading: Bevel gear versions (CAD)
items: v1: Ø12 × 4 mm gear with 23.6° / 33.3° tooth cones and a Ø4.0 mm bore.
v2: grown to Ø16.1 × 6.5 mm with 45° cones, so the two identical gears form a true 1:1 pair at 90°; bore opened to Ø4.5 mm.
Final assembly: a no-bore version of the v2 gear.

sections.heading: Electronics & code
items: Added a piezo buzzer that plays a song in sync with the opening motion of the chest.

items.text: Wrote Arduino code that translates strings into musical notes for the piezo buzzer.
items: Converts strings like "C4" into the correct integer frequency based on A440 tuning.

sections.heading: Result
items: Fully functional desk toy (see the demo video) that uses a custom gear assembly to open the chest in sync with the classic tune from The Legend of Zelda.

sections.heading: What I learned
items: Designing custom bevel gears
Creating dynamic assemblies with multiple moving parts in SolidWorks
Programming servo motors and piezo buzzers in Arduino C++

projects.title: Cost Estimation Tool
projects.card: Board-game cost estimates went from about an hour to about 5 minutes for 4 engineers.

summary.Problem: Give Hasbro games engineers a standard tool to make accurate board-game cost estimates in less time.
summary.My role: Project Engineer Co-op, Hasbro (Games, Play-Doh, NERF); built on my own initiative
summary.Tools: Excel, Power Apps, Power Automate, Power Query, SharePoint
summary.Result: A typical estimate went from about an hour to about 5 minutes

sections.heading: Objective
items: Speed up reference costing: pricing a new board game from the costs of items in existing quotes.

sections.heading: How it works
items: Quote library: the tool reads a library of existing quotes.
Analysis: it analyzes the quote data and breaks it down into individual items.
Cost database: it uploads each item to a cost database on SharePoint.
Estimate: the engineer picks items from dropdowns, such as "deck of 52 cards" or "10 × 10 game board", and the costs fill in automatically.
The final output table is in a project-ready format to share with team members in scrum and gate meetings.
Presented the final working version to employees and leadership from multiple departments at a monthly ToyBox meeting.

sections.heading: Result
items: All 4 games engineers used the tool. A typical estimate went from about an hour to about 5 minutes.
It also gives a more accurate starting cost, which should mean fewer re-estimates and firmer footing when pushing back on vendor quotes.

sections.heading: What I learned
items: Building user-focused Power Apps
Developing Power Automate flows and Power Query scripts
Creating accurate cost estimates from a database of reference costs
Creating SharePoint sites with dynamic lists for large datasets
Advanced Excel formulas, data spills and data validation

projects.title: Flexible Micro-Supercapacitors
projects.card: Technical lead of a 6-person team (Team 13, Micro Charge) that selected materials and planned the process for a flexible micro-supercapacitor.

summary.Problem: Make a micro-scale, mechanically flexible supercapacitor for wearable and implantable devices.
summary.Team: Team 13 "Micro Charge": 6 students; advisor Prof. Yung Joon Jung
summary.My role: Technical lead (team charter): check calculations and verify designs
summary.Status: Research and design done; nothing fabricated yet. Fabrication and testing in Capstone 2

sections.heading: Problem
items: Supercapacitors charge almost instantly and store far more energy than ordinary capacitors, but they are bulky and rigid. A micro-scale, flexible version could power implantable, wearable and compact devices.
Example use case: a smaller, flexible continuous glucose monitor patch. Current monitors are rigid and roughly the size of a walnut.

sections.heading: My role
items: Technical lead, as defined in the team charter: responsible for checking calculations and verifying that designs are valid.
As technical lead, I assigned two teammates to cleanroom and dip-coating training so they can fabricate the prototypes. I do not do cleanroom work myself.
My research topic: which materials are used in supercapacitors today, and why (activated-carbon pore size, carbon nanotubes, graphene, MXene, and aqueous, organic and gel electrolytes).

sections.heading: Material selection
items: Compared electrode, electrolyte and substrate candidates on surface area, conductivity, flexibility, leakage, cost and ease of getting them, then discussed them with the advisor.

Selected design: carbon-nanotube (CNT) electrodes, a PVA gel electrolyte based on phosphoric or sulfuric acid, and a Kapton or PET film as the flexible substrate. CNTs were also already available in the lab.
MXene was dropped: it is easily oxidized and hard to get. A solid gel electrolyte was chosen so nothing can leak.

sections.heading: Planned process
items: Kapton on a silicon carrier wafer → positive photoresist → UV exposure through the lab's existing interdigitated finger masks (10, 20, 50 and 200 µm) → CNT dip or spray coating → lift-off → gel electrolyte and metal terminals → protective encapsulation.

Testing (Spring 2027): capacitor performance and flexibility. The detailed test plan will be set next semester; the team's slides list cyclic voltammetry, charge/discharge, impedance spectroscopy, microscope checks for short circuits and bending fatigue as candidates.

sections.heading: Ethics: chemical leakage
items: I wrote the ethical-issues section of the team's Ethics and Impact memo. I named preventing chemical leakage as the top safety duty for a device worn on or in the body.
This supports the solid gel electrolyte and the protective encapsulation layer in the design.

sections.heading: Timeline
items: Capstone 1 (May–Jun 2026, done): problem statement, team charter, literature research, advisor presentation, Ethics and Impact memo, and final presentation.

Capstone 2 (Jan–Apr 2027, planned): lab, cleanroom, dip-coating and photolithography training; BOM and material orders; initial prototype; characterization; iterative prototypes; final report and presentation.
This page will be updated when there are test results.

projects.title: 3D-Printed Guitar Capo
projects.card: Trial-and-error prints to a print-in-place hinge and ratchet; 7 CAD versions.

summary.Problem: Make a 3D-printed capo for an acoustic guitar that works at more than one fret.
summary.My role: Personal project: design, printing and testing
summary.Result: Fourth version has a working print-in-place hinge and ratchet. It works, but only roughly.

sections.heading: Approach
items: Measured the fretboard at several points, since the neck gets thicker further up.
Commercial capos use metal torsion springs. A plastic print needed a different way to apply pressure.
I did no calculations. It was trial and error: I changed dimensions between prints until it roughly worked.

sections.heading: Iterations
items: 1: two pieces with rubber bands and a flat bar. Hard to attach, and the bar bent, so the middle strings did not sound right.
2: one-piece clip with a rubber band. Easier to attach, but the bar still bent.
3: lever arm on a print-in-place hinge with a ratchet. The hinge fused, and it only fit the first fret.
4: the hinge and ratchet work, and it is easy to attach.
The design went through 7 CAD versions in SolidWorks (v1–v6 and v8).

sections.heading: What I learned
items: Designing print-in-place hinges and a ratchet in SolidWorks
The importance of accounting for deflection in designs

projects.title: Sponge Holder
projects.card: Printed sponge holder that drains into the sink; PLA for prototypes, PETG for the final part.

summary.Problem: Design a 3D-printed sponge holder with a working drainage system that is convenient to use.
summary.Result: Easy-to-use holder that drains directly into the sink without leaving water on the counter

sections.heading: Design process
items: Measured the sponge and used the dimensions to create a 3D model in SolidWorks.

items.text: Printed models in two materials, PETG and PLA.
items: PETG has better temperature and water resistance, so it is the better material for the final product.
PLA prints much faster but does not handle long-term water exposure. It is best for quick prototypes here.

items.text: Iterated on the first model to improve performance.
items: Increased the size of the basin to make the sponge easier to remove.
Added a hook that wraps around the edge of the counter so the holder does not move and water does not spill.

sections.heading: Result
items: A functional, easy-to-use sponge holder that drains directly into my sink without leaving water on the counter.

sections.heading: What I learned
items: Drafting curved surfaces for drainage in SolidWorks
Differences between PETG and PLA filament for 3D printing

projects.title: Custom Shower Installation
projects.card: Built a shower by myself in 2022 to the Massachusetts plumbing code: framing, plumbing, liner, mortar bed and tile.

summary.Problem: Design and install a fully tiled shower to the Massachusetts plumbing code (2022).
summary.My role: Did all of the work myself
summary.Tools: Circular saw, table saw, jig saw, chop saw, hand saws, hammer drill, impact driver, orbital and belt sanders, wet saw, laser level
summary.Result: A functional shower built to code, ready for use in a residential property

sections.heading: Process
items: Researched the Massachusetts plumbing code in effect in 2022 and the relevant building codes to inform the design.
Installed the P-trap, vent pipe, shower valve, PEX supply lines and the other code-required components of the shower's plumbing.

items.text: Built the structural framing with 2x4s and plywood.
items: Tools used: circular saw, table saw, jig saw, chop saw, hammer drill, impact driver, orbital sander.
Installed the insulation, including in the shower bench.
Calculated the best cuts and corners for the PVC liner to use the most material while creating the fewest holes in the liner.
Built a 2×4 screed jig to fill and pitch the mortar bed in the shower basin.
Cut and installed the cement backer board required for tiling.

items.text: Installed tiles on the walls and bench.
items: Used a trowel to apply thinset to the cement board and the back of the tiles.
Cut tiles to size with a wet saw.
Used a laser level and spacers to keep the tiles aligned.
Installed the floor tiles and grouted the walls and floor.

sections.heading: Result
items: A visually appealing, fully functional shower built to the Massachusetts plumbing code, ready for use in a residential property. I did every step myself.

sections.heading: Other home builds
items: Framed an entire kitchen, including the wiring.
Built a staircase.

sections.heading: What I learned
items: Building structural framing
Using many different power tools
Proper tile installation
Installing code-compliant bathroom plumbing
Massachusetts plumbing code requirements

projects.title: Coursework: Measurement Lab & FEA
projects.card: Sensor calibration, time constants, strain-gauge statistics and a wind-tunnel test; a coat hook redesigned from SolidWorks Simulation.

summary.Courses: ME 4505/4506 Measurement & Analysis with Thermal Science Applications (lecture and lab, Spring 2026); Mechanical Engineering Computation & Design; Mechanics of Materials and Dynamics labs
summary.Tools: Arduino DAQ, Excel, SolidWorks Simulation, Abaqus

sections.heading: Measurement & Analysis lab (ME 4505/4506, Spring 2026)
items: Lab 1 and Lab 4 were my individual reports; the other labs and the term project were team work.

Ultrasonic distance sensor (Lab 1): each of us calibrated an Arduino HC-SR04 sensor against a different standard; my report compared all four (NIST gauge blocks, a laser distance meter, a tape measure and a ruler) and checked accuracy and precision against the spec sheet.
Solar cell power curves (Lab 2): designed the experiment, logged cell voltage through the Arduino's 10-bit ADC at two load resistances, and calculated power and efficiency.
Temperature sensors (Lab 3): calibrated a thermocouple and an RTD against a liquid-in-glass thermometer and measured time constants of 0.36 s (thermocouple), 4.9 s (RTD) and 55 s (IC sensor).

items.text: Strain gauges (Lab 4): quarter-, half- and full-bridge Wheatstone circuits read on a Micro-Measurements P3 indicator.
items: Calibration curves, hysteresis, drift and creep for each gauge
30-trial repeatability: chi-squared normality test, outlier test, and the sample size needed for 1% precision (N = 59)
Single-factor ANOVA across the four gauges (F = 24.8 vs. F critical 2.68)
Measured an unknown mass as 1.393 ± 0.589 lb with a full uncertainty analysis
Energy balance (Lab 5): open- and closed-system energy balances on a lamp, using MAX6675 thermocouples, a lux sensor and an Arduino, with measured time constants for the bulb and holder.

Wind tunnel (Lab 6): tested a wind turbine with a pitot-static tube and differential pressure transducer, a hot-wire anemometer and a laser tachometer, then compared horizontal- and vertical-axis turbines' power coefficient against tip-speed ratio (another group tested the second turbine).

Term project (4-person team): calibrated a digital scale against NIST weights (accuracy 1.35%, precision 1.0%), propagated measurement uncertainty, and ran single-factor ANOVA to compare protein per dollar across four burrito restaurants near campus.

sections.heading: Mechanics of Materials and Dynamics labs
items: Tensile, torsion and strain-gauged beam tests.

sections.heading: FEA
items: Coat hook (personal project): designed a 3D-printed coat hook and redesigned it over 3 versions from SolidWorks Simulation static studies until the printed hook held a jacket.
Abaqus: homework in Mechanical Engineering Computation & Design, analyzing beams under several load cases.
